name: The Conservation of Energy
statement: Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.
statementAccent: only changed from one form to another
meaning: The total energy of an isolated system stays constant over time. Energy cannot be made from nothing or made to vanish; whenever it seems to disappear (a rolling ball stopping, a battery running down), it has changed form, into heat, sound, or another store, with the books always balancing.
mechanism: The first law of thermodynamics is the accounting form: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it minus the work it does on its surroundings. Heat and work are both ways of transferring energy, and internal energy is a state function, so energy entering or leaving is tracked exactly with no residue. Deeper still, conservation of energy follows from a symmetry: by Noether's theorem, the fact that the laws of physics do not change over time (time-translation symmetry) is what guarantees energy is conserved.

examples.text: Falling weights turn paddles that stir insulated water; the known mechanical work done appears exactly as a measured temperature rise, energy converting from motion to heat without loss: the experiment that fixed the mechanical equivalent of heat.

At the top of its swing a pendulum's energy is all gravitational potential; at the bottom it is all kinetic; the sum stays constant, with friction merely converting some to heat rather than destroying it.

Burning fuel turns chemical energy stored in bonds into heat and light, and nuclear reactions convert a little mass into large energy: both conserve total energy once every form, mass included, is counted.

variants.name: Mass-energy equivalence
variants.text: Einstein's relation that mass is itself a form of energy, folding mass into the ledger so that conservation of energy and of mass become a single conservation of mass-energy.

variants.name: Noether's theorem
variants.text: The deep result that ties energy conservation to time-translation symmetry: the laws of physics being the same at all times is exactly what makes energy conserved.

whyItMatters: It is among the most strongly established laws in all of physics, underpinning thermodynamics, chemistry, and every branch of engineering. It rules out perpetual-motion machines, disciplines every energy budget from engines to ecosystems, and, through Noether's theorem, reveals conservation laws as the shadows of symmetries.

working.text: when energy seems to vanish, look for the form it took (heat, sound, deformation), since the total must be conserved.
treat any claimed machine that produces energy from nothing as impossible, since it would violate conservation.
apply conservation to a whole isolated system; local energy can rise or fall as energy crosses the boundary.

limits: In all local and terrestrial contexts the law holds without known exception. Its one genuine subtlety is in general relativity: for the universe as a whole, total energy conservation is not always well-defined, because an expanding, dynamic spacetime lacks the time-translation symmetry that conservation rests on. Local energy-momentum conservation still holds, but 'the total energy of the universe is conserved' is not a well-posed statement in cosmology: for instance, light redshifts and loses energy as space expands. This is a matter of careful formulation in curved spacetime, not a failure where the law applies.
misreadings: It does not mean energy stays in one form or that motion never fades: friction converts kinetic energy to heat rather than destroying it. And the cosmological caveat is not a claim that conservation is false; locally and in every laboratory it is unbroken.
origin: Established independently in the 1840s by Julius Robert von Mayer (1842), James Prescott Joule's experiments, and Hermann von Helmholtz's general statement (1847): a classic case of simultaneous discovery; William Rankine first used the phrase 'conservation of energy' in 1850.
